pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–7 years

- **Topic:** Simple Food Chains

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'):** 'describe how animals obtain their food from plants and other animals, using the idea of a simple food chain, and identify and name different sources of food.'

- **Standards — US (no direct K-2 NGSS food-chain PE):** US introduces feeding relationships informally at K-2 (LS2.A: animals depend on plants/other animals for food) but formalises food chains/energy flow later at grade 5 (5-LS2-1, 5-PS3-1). Food chains as an explicit KS1 topic are UK-led — note the divergence honestly.

- **Operational details:** Children build the first big idea in ecology: energy/food passes along a chain that ALWAYS starts with a plant (producer, which makes its own food) and flows to animals (consumers) that eat it and each other. They draw a three-link chain with ARROWS and read the arrow as 'is eaten by / energy flows to'. The arrow direction is the crux — it points from the eaten to the eater, tracking the flow of food-energy, not the act of eating.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete, first causal chain). Success = drawing a 3-organism chain that starts with a plant, using arrows the correct way round, and using 'producer' and 'consumer' correctly — not reversing the arrows or starting a chain with an animal.
bestPractices: Establish the arrow convention explicitly and early: the arrow means 'is eaten by / energy flows to', pointing from food to feeder.
Insist every chain STARTS with a plant (producer) and elicit why (only plants make their own food).
Use local, familiar organisms first (grass→rabbit→fox) before exotic ones.
Draw and read chains both ways — build one, then interpret a given one — to consolidate direction.
Link to prior herbivore/carnivore knowledge so consumer roles make sense.
keyRepresentations: A three-link chain with directional arrows (plant→herbivore→carnivore).
Familiar organism cards to arrange into a chain.
commonMisconceptions: Drawing arrows the wrong way (pointing from the eater to the food).
Starting a food chain with an animal instead of a plant.
Thinking the arrow means 'eats' rather than 'energy/food flows to'.
Believing plants get their food by eating, like animals, rather than making it.
Treating the top predator as the 'start' or most important, rather than the producer.

learn.summary: For ages 6–7, children learn that a simple food chain shows food-energy passing along a sequence that always starts with a plant (a producer that makes its own food) and flows to animals (consumers). The crux is the arrow convention: the arrow means 'is eaten by / energy flows to' and points from the food to the feeder. Activities span building and drawing a three-link chain, interpreting a given labelled chain, checking structure through ordering and matching, and talking through an organism's place in the chain including what happens if the producer is lost. Aligns with UK DfE KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'.

activities.title: Build and arrow a three-link food chain
feedback: If a learner starts the chain with the fox, ask 'Where does the fox's food come from?' and trace back link by link until a plant appears — that is where the chain begins.

If an arrow points the wrong way (from the eater to the food), rename the arrow out loud as 'is eaten by / food goes to' and walk the food-energy from grass into the rabbit into the fox so the arrowhead follows the food.
If a learner is reluctant to begin with grass ('grass isn't really food'), point out that the rabbit's food IS the grass, so the plant is the food source where the chain must start.
Confirm success when the learner draws grass→rabbit→fox with forward arrows, names producer and consumer correctly, and can say why a plant comes first.
activities.rationale: Constructing the chain and the arrows themselves (rather than only recognising a finished one) makes the arrow-direction rule and the plant-first rule a decision the child must make, surfacing the two common reversals so they can be corrected in the moment.
learnerActions: Arrange organism cards (grass, rabbit, fox) into the correct order, left to right.
Draw an arrow between each pair of organisms, pointing from the one that is eaten to the one that eats it.
Say aloud what each arrow means: 'is eaten by / the food and energy pass to the next animal.'
Label each link as 'producer' (the plant) or 'consumer' (each animal).
Explain why the chain must begin with the plant: the grass makes its own food, but the rabbit and fox must eat to get theirs.
activities.intendedInsight: Every food chain starts with a plant that makes its own food, and arrows track food-energy flowing from the eaten to the eater.

activities.title: Interactive chain reference: read the roles and the arrow
feedback: Reinforce the arrow key each time: the arrowhead points to whoever eats.
If a learner reads the arrow as 'eats', restate it as 'is eaten by / food goes to' and have them re-read the chain in that direction.
activities.rationale: A clean labelled reference consolidates the vocabulary and the arrow key. This is a reading/interpretation scaffold rather than independent construction, so it supports but does not replace the building task.
learnerActions: Tap or point to each organism to reveal its role: 'I eat… / I am eaten by…' and whether it is a producer or consumer.
Tap or point to each arrow to reveal that it means 'is eaten by / energy flows to'.
Retell the chain in your own words, naming producer and consumer and reading each arrow correctly.
activities.intendedInsight: The arrow carries a fixed meaning ('is eaten by / energy flows to') and each organism has a role (producer or consumer) that stays consistent across the chain.

activities.title: Order the chain and choose the starting rule
feedback: For ordering errors, ask what each animal's food is and trace back to the plant.
For the 'starts with' item, confirm plants make their own food so they are the source everything else depends on.
For arrow-direction items, restate the arrow as 'is eaten by'.
activities.rationale: Ordering, selection and matching efficiently check the structure of the chain. These response formats confirm recognition of the rule; they do not require the learner to draw arrows live, so pair them with the building activity for independent construction.
learnerActions: Put a scrambled set of organisms (grass, rabbit, fox) into the correct chain order.
Answer: 'What does every food chain start with?' and choose the plant/producer.
Answer an arrow-direction item: which way does the arrow point between two organisms?
Match each organism to its label: 'producer' or 'consumer'.
activities.intendedInsight: A food chain has a fixed structure — producer first, then consumers — and the arrow direction and role labels can be identified reliably.

activities.title: Talk through an animal's place in the chain
feedback: If the learner cannot name what comes before an animal, prompt 'what is its food?' and connect that to the previous link.
Steer every trace-back to the producer so the plant-first idea is reinforced through talk.
For the 'what if the grass died out' prompt, help the learner reason that the rabbit would lose its food and the fox in turn would lose the rabbit — the chain depends on the producer.
activities.rationale: A spoken walk-along the chain can reinforce the 'before/after' relationships and the chain's dependence on the producer through dialogue. For this age, pair it with building or seeing the chain drawn, since an abstract spoken sequence can be harder to hold than a visible chain.
learnerActions: Take the part of one animal in the chain (e.g. the rabbit).
Answer: 'What do I eat?' and 'Who eats me?'
Name what comes before you (your food) and after you (your eater) in the chain.
Trace the whole chain back to the plant that makes its own food.
Consider what would happen to the fox if all the grass died out, and explain how the whole chain depends on the plant at the start.
activities.intendedInsight: Each animal sits between what it eats and what eats it; following those links backwards always reaches a plant, and because every animal ultimately depends on the producer, losing the plant affects the whole chain.

constraints: Establish the arrow convention explicitly and early: the arrow means 'is eaten by / energy flows to', pointing from food to feeder.
Insist every chain starts with a plant (producer) and elicit why — plants make their own food, while animals have to eat other living things.
Use local, familiar organisms first (grass→rabbit→fox) before exotic ones.
Build chains both ways: construct one, then interpret a given one, to consolidate arrow direction.
Link to prior herbivore/carnivore knowledge so consumer roles make sense.

Reading/interpretation activities (labelled reference, ordering, matching) confirm recognition but do not require the learner to construct arrows independently; include at least one task where the learner draws the chain and arrows themselves.
Spoken walk-throughs support relational understanding but should accompany, not replace, a visible or drawn chain at this age.

Address the common misconceptions directly: reversed arrows, starting with an animal, reading the arrow as 'eats', believing plants eat for their food rather than making it, and treating the top predator as the start/most important.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The building activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because the DfE KS1 standard supports the objective/topic but does not directly evidence the construction-surfaces-reversals rationale; the curriculum alignment is noted here instead.

The source noted a US/UK divergence: NGSS introduces feeding relationships informally at K-2 but formalises food chains and energy flow at grade 5 (5-LS2-1, 5-PS3-1); explicit KS1 food-chain teaching is UK-led. Adjust expectations for US learners accordingly.

The original claim that '3D adds nothing over a flat builder' was a catalog fit comment, not an established pedagogical law; it has been softened/omitted. A food chain is commonly represented as a flat directional sequence, which is sufficient for this objective, but this does not prove other media cannot help.

The original 'bench checks flow / animates food flowing backwards and is rejected' describes an optional interactive mechanism; retained as an example of corrective feedback, not as a required mechanism.

The dependency/knock-on reasoning (what happens if the producer is lost) comes from the saved assessment's probeDeeper and full-response level; it has been reinstated as an extension in the dialogue activity to preserve that assessment depth.
The comparative claim that a spoken sequence is harder to hold than a visible chain is kept only in qualified form and is not independently verified.

probeDeeper: If the arrow means 'is eaten by', who is eaten by the fox in your chain?
Where does the grass get its own food from?
Could a food chain ever start with a fox? Why not?
What would happen to the fox if all the grass died out?
assess.correctAnswer: Arrows point grass → rabbit → fox, and an arrow means 'is eaten by' / the food and its energy pass to the next animal. The chain starts with grass because a plant is a producer — it makes its own food using sunlight, so it is the source of food and energy that everything else depends on; animals are consumers and cannot make their own food.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The arrow shows who eats who, so it points from the fox to what it eats' — reads the arrow as 'eats' and reverses the whole chain.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rename the arrow out loud as 'is eaten by / food goes to'; walk energy from grass into the rabbit into the fox so the arrowhead follows the food.
errorPatterns.distractor: The arrows should point from the fox to the rabbit to the grass, to show who eats who.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws fox → rabbit → grass, or says the arrow 'points to its dinner'.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The chain starts with the biggest, strongest animal' — puts the top predator first.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what the fox's energy ultimately came from; trace back until you reach the thing that makes its own food — the plant — and start there.
errorPatterns.distractor: The chain should start with the fox, because it is the biggest and strongest.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Begins the chain with the fox; treats 'first' as most powerful rather than the food source.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Food chains start with an animal — grass isn't really food' — does not see the plant as the producer/food source.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish plants as producers that make food; the rabbit's food IS the grass, so the plant is where the chain must begin.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reluctant to begin with grass; says food chains start with 'something that eats'.

responseLevels.gap: Reverses the arrows or starts the chain with an animal; cannot say what the arrow means.
responseLevels.full: Draws correct direction, explains the arrow as food/energy passing to the eater, justifies the plant-first rule by producers making their own food, and predicts a knock-on effect if the producer is lost.
responseLevels.partial: Draws the chain grass-first with forward arrows but explains the arrow only as 'eats', or cannot say why a plant must come first.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'A rabbit eats grass, and a fox eats the rabbit. I want you to draw this as a food chain with arrows, and tell me what each arrow means. Then tell me: why must the chain start with the grass and not with the fox?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks the arrow means 'eats' draws them backwards (fox → rabbit → grass). A child who thinks the 'biggest, strongest' animal comes first starts with the fox. Only a child using the food-source/energy-flow idea puts the plant first with forward-pointing arrows — the two errors give visibly different drawings.
